deep.reconstruction:
PROBLEM (identification from the formulas): among all homogeneous solids of revolution of given mass (volume) M, find the one that exerts the greatest attraction, along the axis, on a point at the origin on its surface. Then compare it with a sphere of the same mass. This is the classical 'solid of greatest attraction'. The calculations are in pencil, upside down beneath the heading of a letter to his father dated Göttingen, 18 Dec 1850.

SETUP (stated more fully than on the page). Take the axis of revolution as the x-axis, the attracted point at the origin, and let y(x) be the radius of the cross-section at abscissa x.
- A ring of radius r and thickness dr at abscissa x contributes 2π r x dr/(x²+r²)^{3/2} to the axial attraction.
- Integrating over 0 ≤ r ≤ y gives 2π(1 − x/√(x²+y²)) per unit dx.
- So the attraction is A = 2π∫(1 − x/√(x²+y²)) dx.
- Riemann's first lines ∫ ∂√(y²+x²)/∂x dx = ∫ x dx/√(y²+x²) are exactly the non-trivial part of this.
- The mass is M = π∫ y² dx (the line '∫ y² dx').

VARIATION. Maximise A subject to fixed M. With a multiplier λ, the line '... y δy + ... = 0' expresses
 x y δy/(x²+y²)^{3/2} − λ y δy = 0, i.e. x/(x²+y²)^{3/2} = const.
Hence (x²+y²)^{3/2} = c·x, written on the page as y²+x² = m x^{2/3}, so y² = m x^{2/3} − x².

EXTENT. The curve meets the axis again where m x^{2/3} = x², i.e. at x = a = m^{3/4}. This is the upper limit written.

MASS (labelled 'Maximum').
M = π∫_0^{m^{3/4}} (m x^{2/3} − x²) dx = π[(3/5) m x^{5/3} − x³/3] at x = a.
Since m a^{5/3} = a^{4/3}·a^{5/3} = a³, this equals π(3/5 − 1/3)a³ = (4π/15)a³ (written as (2/15)x³·2π).
Therefore a = ∛(15M/(4π)), which is written in the left margin.

ATTRACTION. On the surface x/√(x²+y²) = x/√(m x^{2/3}) = m^{−1/2} x^{2/3}.
So A = 2π∫_0^a (1 − m^{−1/2}x^{2/3}) dx = 2π[a − m^{−1/2}(3/5)a^{5/3}].
With m^{−1/2} = a^{−2/3} this is 2π(a − (3/5)a) = 2π·(2/5)a = (4π/5)a.
The page shows m^{−1/2}(3/5)x^{5/3} = (3/5)x, times 2π.

COMPARISON WITH THE SPHERE (second brace).
- A sphere of radius x with the point on its surface has M = (4π/3)x³, so x = ∛(3M/(4π)); both forms are on the page.
- Its attraction is M/x² = (4π/3)x.
- The same value follows from the slice method: with y² = 2rx − x² one gets 2π∫_0^{2r}(1 − √(x/2r)) dx = 2π(2r − (4/3)r) = (4π/3)r, apparently the last lines '(2/3)x·4π' etc.

IMPLIED CONCLUSION (not written). The ratio of the optimal attraction to the sphere's is (4π/5)(15M/4π)^{1/3} / [(4π/3)(3M/4π)^{1/3}] = (3/5)·5^{1/3} = 3/5^{2/3} ≈ 1.026. That is, the optimal solid beats the sphere by about 2.6%.

UNCLEAR LINE. The line '∫ φx dx, ∫ (1/φ² − x²) dx' seems to be a trial general parametrisation (y² + x² expressed through a function φ); it cannot be reconstructed with certainty.
errors: No mathematical errors detected in the legible parts.
The volume is written as (2/15)x³·2π; this correctly equals (4π/15)a³.
The upper limit m^{3/4} is correct.
Some lines (the φ-line, '½x²·4π', and the x³/3 · 4π/3 line) are too fragmentary to check.

results.what: Meridian curve of the homogeneous solid of revolution of given mass with maximal axial attraction at a surface point: (x²+y²)^{3/2} = c x, i.e. y² + x² = m x^{2/3}
results.modern_name: Solid of greatest attraction (isoperimetric problem in the calculus of variations)
results.usually_credited_to: Silvabelle (1760s) and John Playfair (1809, 'On the solids of greatest attraction'); standard 19th-century textbook exercise (e.g. in Todhunter)

results.what: Volume (4π/15)a³ and attraction (4π/5)a of the optimal solid, and comparison with the sphere ((4π/3)r³, (4π/3)r): ratio 3/5^{2/3} ≈ 1.026
results.modern_name: Optimal solid's attraction exceeds the sphere's by about 2.6%

deep.surprise_reason: A classical, well-known calculus-of-variations exercise (solid of greatest attraction), worked correctly by the 24-year-old student Riemann as scratch work on a letter sheet. It is of biographical interest only.

checkable.asserts: Volume of the optimal solid equals (4π/15)a³ with a = m^{3/4} (result 0).
Axial attraction of the optimal solid equals (4π/5)a (result 0).
Attraction of a disc of radius y at axial distance x (result 0).
Sphere of radius r attracts a surface point with 4πr/3 (result 0).
Ratio of optimal to spherical attraction for equal mass ≈ 1.026 = 3/5^(2/3).
Euler–Lagrange condition; setting it to zero gives x/(x²+y²)^{3/2} = const.

transcription_corrections: '= (2/15)x³·2π = M' should be read as π(3/5 − 1/3)x³ = (4π/15)x³ = M.
The second attraction line is best read as ∫_0^{m^{3/4}} m^{−1/2}x^{2/3} dx = m^{−1/2}(3/5)x^{5/3} = (3/5)x, giving A = 2π(x − (3/5)x).
The marginal label read as 'Paraboloid [?]' is more likely 'Kugelform' / 'Kugel' (sphere), since the bracketed lines compute M = (4π/3)x³ and x = ∛(3M/4π).
The upper limit is m^{3/4}, as transcribed (consistent with the curve meeting the axis at x^{4/3} = m).
'... y δy + ... = 0' is the variational condition x y δy/(x²+y²)^{3/2} − λ y δy = 0.
